extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic, philosophy of science, and scientifically-minded readers interested in the theory of induction
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and evaluating criteria distinguishing genuine induction (generalization from experience) from mere description/colligation, mathematical parity reasoning, or invention; concerned with what makes inductive inferences legitimate, testable, and predictive. Useful for judging or producing arguments that claim inductive support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction properly so called
rubrics_metrics.description: Generalization from Experience: inferring from some individual instances in which a phenomenon is observed that it occurs in all instances of a certain class — i.e. in all which resemble the former in the material circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the core definition: induction infers something unobserved from something observed. It presupposes a distinction between material and immaterial circumstances (which must be determined) and rests on the assumption of parallel cases/uniformity of nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generalization must contain more than sum of particulars
rubrics_metrics.description: A real generalization (induction) contains more than the sum of the special propositions from which it is inferred; merely saying 'all known X' is not induction unless it commits to X beyond the known cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: saying 'all animals have a nervous system' as a law (predicting in unknown species) is induction; saying 'all known animals' is merely enumerative. Legitimate induction adds content beyond the enumerated instances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency determined by number and nature of instances, not exhaustiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Legitimacy of a generalization does not generally require examination of every known instance; it depends on the number and nature of the instances examined, not on their being the whole of known cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: demanding exhaustive verification of every known species to justify a law. Correct practice: evaluate representativeness and relevant variety of instances rather than mere completeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish colligation/description from induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Colligation (description) is the piecing together of partial observations into a single representation (e.g. navigator concluding 'island' or Kepler representing planetary positions as an ellipse); this sums up observed facts but does not infer unobserved facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat a successful descriptive formulation as an inductive proof. Examples: navigator sailing round land (description), Kepler's ellipse as representation of observed positions (description). Only when one infers unobserved intermediate or future positions does induction occur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction is inference enabling explanation and prediction
rubrics_metrics.description: The proper purposes of induction are explanation and prediction — determining conditions under which similar facts may be expected to recur; mere description does not serve these purposes by itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate candidate inductive claims by whether they assert unobserved facts or predictive conditions. Descriptive formulas that merely represent known observations cannot, by themselves, be considered inductive proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction requires proof/tests and inductive canons
rubrics_metrics.description: Induction is a form of proof (inferring unobserved from observed) and therefore requires appropriate tests or canons to establish its legitimacy; inductive logic’s role is to provide such tests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns: accepting conjectures because they provide a neat description without subjecting them to inductive tests. Good practice: apply rules/tests (e.g., methods of agreement/difference — discussed elsewhere in the work) to assess inductive strength.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invention (introduction of new conceptions) is not equivalent to induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Introducing a new conception to connect facts is an act of invention; invention may be used in description or to formulate inductive hypotheses, but it is not itself the essence of induction (which is proof/inference).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware of conflating creative hypothesis-generation with inductive justification. The presence of a novel conception (e.g., 'ellipse', 'wheels') does not make an operation inductive unless it is used to infer unobserved facts and is testably supported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction presupposes colligation but is not identical with it
rubrics_metrics.description: Colligation (grouping observations under a conception) is a necessary preparation for induction — we must represent phenomena as wholes to have cases for induction — but colligation alone is not induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation should check whether descriptive colligation has been turned into an inductive inference (adds unobserved claims) and whether the colligation supplies a usable basis for inductive testing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical 'induction by parity of reasoning' is not genuine induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical generalization where the truth is shown by demonstration or parity of reasoning (e.g., proving a theorem for one diagram then arguing the same proof applies generally) is not induction in the empirical sense because the general truth is obtained by demonstrative evidence, not inference from observed particulars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conflate mathematical proof or a priori reasoning with empirical induction. Example: proving geometric properties for a particular figure and deriving general theorem by demonstrative reasoning is 'induction by parity' but lacks the inferential character of empirical induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical extrapolation requires a priori grounds or demonstrable mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: When extrapolating patterns (e.g., algebraic series, binomial coefficients) from a finite number of calculated terms, one should have a priori considerations or demonstrable reasons showing the mode of formation will persist; blind extrapolation can lead to false results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess extrapolations for underlying rationale (combinatorial arguments, mechanism) rather than relying solely on observed pattern across a few cases. Newton's discovery of the binomial theorem is cited as likely underpinned by such a priori insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis formation is tentative and requires testing
rubrics_metrics.description: The selection of a conception or hypothesis to represent facts is typically tentative — a succession of guesses, many rejected until a skillful guess fits the observations; the guess must then be tested against additional facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good practice: treat hypotheses as provisional; test predicted unobserved consequences and reject or refine hypotheses that fail. Example: Kepler tried many paths before ellipse; successful hypothesis is a 'skillful guess' validated by agreement with data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different descriptions can be all correct as approximations
rubrics_metrics.description: Successive, conflicting general expressions used to colligate observed facts (e.g., circular or epicyclic descriptions of planetary motion) may each be correct representations of the facts as they were known at the time; such descriptions can be useful approximations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating descriptive models, consider their intended scope and precision. Older, simpler models can be valuable for rough approximations even if later superseded for explanatory truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanations (causal theories) are not mutually compatible approximations — only one can be true
rubrics_metrics.description: Whereas different descriptions may be equally serviceable, conflicting explanations or causal accounts (e.g., vortices vs. Newtonian gravitation) cannot all be true; explanatory claims are evaluated on truth, not mere descriptive adequacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between models useful for representation and rival theories that make incompatible claims about causes; explanatory claims require stricter inductive support and can be falsified by counterevidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colligation must be consistent with observed facts
rubrics_metrics.description: A conception introduced to connect observations must at least be consistent with the facts it purports to represent; consistency with observations is the minimal requirement for a descriptive colligation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check that the proposed conception reproduces known data; consistency alone does not amount to inductive proof, but inconsistency falsifies the colligation. Use empirical checks of fit to observed particulars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction assumes uniformity of nature / parallel cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Every instance of induction implicitly assumes that there are parallel cases in nature — that what happens once will, under sufficient similarity of circumstances, happen again; this assumption is warranted by experience but must be recognized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating inductive inferences, make explicit the assumption of relevant similarity and consider whether the asserted parallels are justified. Identifying which circumstances are 'material' is central to assessing this assumption.
